chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ahmad ibn al-Walid (may God be pleased with him) narrated that Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar quoted Ahmad ibn Abi Abdullah al-Barqi, on the authority of Isma'il ibn Mihran, on the authority of Ubays ibn Hisham al-Nashiri, on the authority of someone who linked it up through other narrators to Abi Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

Recitation of the Quran is of three types: A man who recited the Quran and made it his merchandise, using it to approach the kings and to act haughty with the people; and a man who recited the Quran, memorized its letters but neglected its bounds; and a man who recited the Quran and applied the medicine of the Quran to the illness of his heart, so he stayed awake with it at night, and felt thirst with it during the day, and stood in prayer with it in his mosques, and kept his back away from his bed with it. By those, Allah the Mighty, the Omnipotent, wards off calamity; by those, Allah takes revenge from the enemies; and by those, Allah sends down rain from the sky. I swear by God that those are the reciters of the Quran, more scarce than red sulfur.

key_terms.الْكَبْرِيتَ الْأَحْمَرَ: red sulfur (used as a metaphor for rarity/scarcity)

ai.seo_question: What are the three types of Quran reciters according to Imam al-Baqir (AS)?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq presents this tripartite classification to distinguish between the utilitarian, the superficial, and the transformative engagement with the Quran, emphasizing that true recitation requires internalizing the text as a cure for the heart's ailments. The third group’s dedication—marked by night prayer (Qiyam) and vigilance—positions them as the means through which God averts calamity and sends rain, highlighting the cosmic impact of sincere devotion. This reflects the Shia emphasis on the unity of knowledge (Ilm) and action (Amal), where recitation is incomplete without spiritual and practical implementation.
